items.title: Monohydrate is the studied form
items.body:
Most creatine research uses one form: creatine monohydrate. A 2021 expert review counts more than 500 peer-reviewed papers on creatine supplementation.

No other form has been shown to beat it. So the first word to look for on any label, powder or gummy, is monohydrate.
items.evidence: Expert review, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2021
items.alt: A wooden scoop of white powder beside a glass of water and a green apple
items.evidence_label: Expert review · Antonio et al., JISSN 2021

items.title: A small daily amount works too
items.body:
You don't need a loading phase. In a classic muscle biopsy study, a high-dose load raised muscle creatine about 20% in 6 days.

A low daily dose reached the same 20% rise by day 28, just more slowly. Steady daily intake gets you there.

chart.title: Rise in muscle creatine
chart.source: Hultman et al., J Appl Physiol 1996. 31 men; 20 g/day for 6 days vs 3 g/day for 28 days, muscle total creatine.

items.evidence_label: Human study · Hultman et al., J Appl Physiol 1996

items.title: Gummies were tested in a trial
items.body:
Does creatine still work in a gummy? A 10-week randomized trial gave 32 female beach volleyball athletes creatine gummies daily or no supplement.

The gummy group jumped higher and changed direction faster. Lean mass did not differ between groups. One small trial, but a real one.
items.evidence: Randomized controlled trial, J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 2026
items.alt: A volleyball resting on sand beside a net post at sunset

items.title: With training, more lean mass
items.body:
A meta-analysis of 22 trials pooled 721 adults with average ages of 57 to 70. All did resistance training two to three times a week.

Adding creatine gave 1.37 kg more lean mass than training alone, plus stronger chest and leg presses. The key word is training.
items.evidence: Meta-analysis (22 RCTs, 721 adults), Open Access J Sports Med 2017

chart.title: Older adults who trained: 22 trials
chart.source: Chilibeck PD et al. Open Access J Sports Med 2017;8:213-226. Creatine vs placebo during resistance training.

items.evidence_label: Meta-analysis of 22 RCTs · Chilibeck et al., 2017

items.title: Women see small, real gains
items.body:
Evidence in women has been thinner. A 2026 meta-analysis gathered 34 studies of women who exercise or train, with 692 participants.

It found small positive effects on strength and power. The authors rate certainty as low, so expect modest changes, not dramatic ones.
items.evidence: Systematic review and meta-analysis, Front Nutr 2026
items.alt: Light sage dumbbells, a rolled linen mat and a water bottle by a window
items.evidence_label: Meta-analysis (34 studies in women) · Lin et al., 2026

items.title: No head-to-head with powder
items.body:
The gummy trial compared creatine gummies with no supplement. We found no published trial comparing gummies with powder directly.

So the case for gummies rests on the same monohydrate research, plus convenience. The amount per serving is what to check.
items.evidence: Evidence gap: Europe PMC search 2026-10-08, no gummy vs powder trial to cite
items.alt: Printed research papers, reading glasses and a green apple on linen
items.evidence_label: Literature check · no gummy vs powder trial found

items.title: Well tolerated in healthy adults
items.body:
The ISSN position stand concludes that creatine is safe and well tolerated in healthy people, in studies lasting up to five years.

Taking medication or managing a kidney condition? Ask your doctor first. Daily use is what the research tested.
items.evidence: Position stand, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017
items.alt: A glass of water and a small dish of pale green gummies on a travertine counter
items.evidence_label: Position stand · Kreider et al., JISSN 2017
